PyCC provides a broad range of molecular properties such as analytic first and second energy derivatives including gradients, Hessians, polarizabilities and atomic polar tensors, as well as non-energy-derivative properties, such as velocity-gauge atomic polar tensors and diagonal Born-Oppenheimer corrections, plus dynamic linear response functions, and excitation energies. The package includes a number of unique capabilities, such as real-time CC propagation (up through CC3), atomic axial tensors for simulating vibrational circular dichroism spectra at the MP2, CID, CISD, and CCSD levels, and local correlation methods including perturbation-aware correlation domains. The code is designed around a shared Wavefunction base and a method-agnostic derivative layer that enables a new method to inherit the full energy-derivative property set once it supplies its reduced densities and their first-order responses. PyCC is fully open source and available on GitHub under the BSD 3-clause license.

papers.title: Recovering Parallelism under Fixed Numerical References in Quantized LLM Decoders
papers.abstract: Splitting a quantized decoder at a physical attention-view boundary can break projection groups that already match a fixed numerical reference. LOCAL retains those groups, partitions queries by physical view inside attention, and rejoins the outputs in query order. Owned score rows survive native-buffer reuse, and commit supplies the key-value (KV) and consumer state for the next call. At a fixed 32B attention-view crossing on A5000 with frozen proposals, LOCAL reduces verification-through-commit time by 21.56% against SIMPLE (the whole-call splitting baseline). This supporting endpoint covers 12 paired time blocks (95% CI [20.21%, 22.83%]). In the primary noncrossing history, both arms retain the four-column projection and the estimated reduction is 0.43% [-1.13%, 2.01%]. This comparison measures the two implementations when neither fragments the projection group. Across two fixed 8B conversations under target-only decoding, the primary equal-weight estimate was a 1.44% reduction in response-plus-reset time (95% CI [-0.82%, 3.85%]). Separate studies with SIMPLE fixed report request-time reductions from few-column execution (C4) and packing of admitted groups (P4); the RTX C4 contrasts are descriptive secondary results. The fixed-crossing result demonstrates that attention can observe its physical-view boundaries while projection retains parallel work under the same numerical reference.

papers.title: Where to Look Is Not How to Fix: Pre-Denoising Diagnostics and Modality-Dependent Control in Diffusion Composition
papers.abstract: Understanding compositional failures in text-to-image diffusion requires identifying both where stress is detectable and how intervention changes the output. We study these questions through a controlled anchor--stress protocol that jointly evaluates text-encoder diagnostics and denoiser interventions. We introduce a text-only Compositional Stress Index (CSI), which separates common from rare compositions across SD1.5, SDXL, and the SD3 text path and provides an upstream diagnostic coordinate. A matched six-prompt localization study links intervention location to distinct outcomes: residual-minimizing embedding adapters improve representation fit, while downstream cross-attention intervention increases color hit rate (CHR) by 0.0272. Across SD1.5 and SDXL denoiser blocks, the largest positive signed diagnostic-accessibility mean occurs at the deep encoder, whereas selective boost has its largest positive mean CHR response at decoder blocks. Selective subtraction and broad ablation reveal further modality- and architecture-dependent responses, including a substantial CHR decrease when SDXL decoder cross-attention is broadly ablated. We find a diagnosis-control dissociation under our controlled attribute-object composition setting: compositional defects are diagnosable before denoising, but the representation coordinate that exposes risk is not necessarily the coordinate or modality that improves generation.

papers.title: Study of the Ultra-Long GRB 220627A: Exploring a Possible Blue Supergiant Collapsar Origin
papers.abstract: Ultra-long gamma-ray bursts (ul-GRBs) challenge standard collapsar models because their extreme durations require central engines active for $\sim10^{3}-10^{4}$ s. While the prompt spectral evolution of typical GRBs is difficult to resolve due to their short durations, ul-GRBs provide a unique opportunity to study spectral evolution on extended timescales. We present a time-resolved spectroscopic study of GRB 220627A, one of the most luminous ul-GRBs known ($E_{\rm iso}\sim10^{54}$ erg, $T_{90}>1000$ s), consisting of two bright emission episodes separated by $\sim600$ s quiescent interval. Using a novel HOP algorithm-based segmentation method, we identify optimal time intervals for time-resolved spectroscopy. A Comptonized power-law (CPL) model well describes the prompt emission ($\sim 10$ keV-40 MeV) across all timescales. Fermi-GBM spectroscopy reveals a transition from a hard, slow-cooling synchrotron spectrum ($α_{\rm I}=-0.70$) during episode-I to a softer, fast-cooling synchrotron spectrum ($α_{\rm II}=-1.29$) during episode-II. This evolution closely resembles that of the magnetar-candidate GRB 091024A, highlighting a potential progenitor degeneracy based solely on spectral evolution. However, the extreme isotropic-equivalent energy exceeds the maximum energy available from magnetar spin-down, strongly favouring a blue supergiant (BSG) collapsar origin. The prolonged activity and multi-episode structure are naturally explained by sustained accretion through an extended stellar envelope. Our results demonstrate that ul-GRBs can display magnetar-like spectral evolution while being powered by BSG collapsars. GRB 220627A highlights the need for combining time-resolved spectroscopy with energetic constraints to distinguish between progenitor scenarios and understand the physical origin of ul-GRBs.

papers.title: Central algebraic cohomology of Galois gerbes and its abelianization
papers.abstract: We study central algebraic cohomology and its abelianization for Galois gerbes over local fields of characteristic zero and over number fields. The coefficients consist of a connected reductive group and a central subgroup that need not be finite or connected. We construct a canonical abelian group structure on abelian central cohomology. When the gerbe admits a morphism from Kaletha's rigid gerbe, we obtain a fiber product formula for this group in terms of rigid cohomology and homomorphisms from the band to the central subgroup. Over number fields, abelianization and localization at the real places recover the full central cohomology set. We obtain explicit formulas for Kottwitz's local and global gerbes and for Fargues's extended Kottwitz gerbe.

papers.title: Antipodal Self-Duality for Generalized Fishnets from Integrability
papers.abstract: Antipodal self-duality (ASD) is a remarkable property that relates an amplitude to itself, after performing a suitable kinematic map and reversing the letters of the symbol (more precisely, acting with the antipode of the Hopf algebra of the de Rham analogs of multiple polylogarithms). ASD has been seen in only one process in planar $\mathcal{N}=4$ super-Yang-Mills theory, and its physical origin is unknown, motivating a search for ASD in other contexts. Recently, ASD was found to hold for square fishnet integrals in a strongly-deformed version of planar $\mathcal{N}=4$. In this paper, we investigate the properties of polynomials in ladder integrals under the ASD transformation that leaves the square fishnet invariant. Our basic building blocks are determinants of certain matrices of ladder integrals, that are labeled by partitions or Young diagrams, and automatically obey the Steinmann relations. We employ integrability-based representations of such determinants, which are essentially matrix-model integrals, and the theory of symmetric polynomials to find many more ASD quantities -- linear combinations of determinants whose coefficients are expressed using the combinatorics of partitions. As a byproduct, we provide an alternate proof that square fishnet integrals obey ASD.

papers.title: Made to Measure: Designing Image Watermarks to Specification
papers.abstract: Image watermarking enables provenance and attribution, but practical deployments must jointly satisfy robustness, false-positive rate (FPR), image quality, and latency requirements. Existing watermarking methods offer complementary robustness against different attacks, making their composition attractive for broader protection. However, combining watermarks introduces interference, distortion, decoding overhead, and additional verification paths that share the same FPR budget. We propose TAILOR, a request-conditioned watermark composition framework with three stages: (1) offline characterization models fragment recovery, distortion, latency, and composition interactions across embedding strengths; (2) joint configuration selection uses satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) to jointly optimize fragment selection, continuous embedding strengths, embedding order, and geometric recovery while minimizing predicted distortion; and (3) live calibration validates candidate configurations on user images and refines inaccurate offline predictions to improve deployment success. Across 7,321 distinct deployment requests spanning five scenarios and 20 attack settings, TAILOR achieves 96.21% scenario-averaged request satisfaction with a mean PSNR of 41.02 dB, demonstrating its effectiveness in meeting diverse deployment requirements while maintaining high image fidelity. Code is available at https://github.com/aaFrostnova/Tailor.

papers.title: A Pogorelov-type estimate for the real twisted Monge-Ampère equation
papers.abstract: We establish a Pogorelov type interior $C^2$ estimate for the real twisted Monge-Ampere equation without assuming uniform ellipticity. This equation is fully nonlinear and elliptic, but is neither concave nor a function of the eigenvalues of the Hessian, so the standard techniques for interior second-derivative estimates do not directly apply. Building on the partial Legendre transform formulation of Streets and Warren, we derive a differential identity for the associated positive-definite matrix $W(D^2u)$ and use some linear algebra to control the third-order terms arising in the maximum principle argument. As an application, we prove a Liouville theorem for entire split convex solutions with quadratic growth, extending the rigidity theorem of Streets and Warren by replacing their uniform ellipticity hypothesis with suitable quadratic growth assumptions.

papers.title: Transcending Algebraic Geometry
papers.abstract: We give an exposition of some of the ideas leading up to Jacob Tsimerman's groundbreaking work developing the theory of o-minimal definability in arithmetic and algebraic geometry.

papers.title: A question of Ulam and a theorem of de Rham
papers.abstract: We generalize de Rham's decomposition theorem to proper metric spaces: every proper metric space has a unique decomposition as the product of a Euclidean space and a finite or countable pointed $\ell^2$-product of nontrivial irreducible non-Euclidean factors. A slightly weaker unique decomposition statement is verified for general complete metric spaces. We use this to resolve a question of Ulam on the uniqueness of square roots of complete metric spaces.

papers.title: More RLBWT Tricks
papers.abstract: Indexes based on $k$-mers can beat BWT-based indexes when the former take advantage of unitigs in de Bruijn graphs. In this paper we consider ways in which BWT-based indexes can do that as well, or even better. In particular, we consider MEM-finding between human chromosome 19s, where we can achieve a five- to sevenfold speedup over plain backward search, or a two- to threefold speedup over plain backward search with latency hiding, for about twice the space.

papers.title: Non-Hermitian Yang--Mills Connections with Vanishing Chern Classes
papers.abstract: We construct non-flat non-Hermitian Yang--Mills connections with vanishing Chern classes whose induced and conjugate-dual holomorphic bundles are both stable, giving a negative answer to Kaledin and Verbitsky's flatness question even under these stability assumptions. We also give negative answers to their questions about the étaleness and bijectivity of the harmonic-class map. The examples are explicit connections on smoothly trivial rank-two bundles over projective Kähler surfaces and admit explicit positive harmonic metrics. For the family of fixed stable bundles studied here, the harmonic-class map is surjective. Every fibre contains exactly one flat point, but some fibres also contain positive-dimensional families of non-flat connections. The entire flat locus is a smooth component mapped biholomorphically onto the target. For a range of parameters, we determine the complete reduced analytic germ at a distinguished nonunitary flat point. It has two smooth branches of different dimensions whose intersection contains two-sided stable points arbitrarily close to that point. Finally, a single fibre of the pair of holomorphic projections contains infinitely many flat classes and an embedded copy of $\CC^*$ with exactly two flat members. Thus the two holomorphic isomorphism classes together do not determine flatness.

papers.title: Beyond Accuracy: Prefix-Invariant Realizations of Low-Precision Fast Matrix Multiplication
papers.abstract: Fast matrix multiplication saves multiplications through exact cancellation, but rounding sums that mix token rows can leave contributions from later tokens in earlier language model outputs. This threatens prefix invariance, which likelihood scoring and batched inference rely on: an output must depend only on its allowed prefix. On Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, two fast FP8 realizations repaired to near-bf16 accuracy, and the existing fast kernel FalconGEMM, change answers when only text outside the allowed prefix is replaced: on 4.17--10.00% of OpenBookQA items scored by likelihood and 39.6--51.8% of NQ-open questions answered in a batch. Accuracy thus does not certify prefix invariance, and the stability criteria we analyze cannot tell realizations apart: across all 512 sign variants of two-level Strassen the criteria stay constant while teacher-forced perplexities span a 772.4$\times$ range on the same model. We therefore construct certified realizations of two-level Strassen on bounded integer codes that quantize token rows independently, then mix and cancel exactly before rescaling, using 49 block multiplications instead of 64. Our certificate guarantees bitwise equality to a prescribed row-local classical int8 operator at the same quantization specification, so every certified realization inherits its prefix invariance. Certification thus turns realization choice into a pure cost decision: which certified realization runs can no longer change any output. With optimized kernels, certified realizations run faster than classical int8 on an NVIDIA H20, and in the SGLang serving engine they raise throughput over its FP8 path by 1.2--5.6% on four models.

papers.title: Quantum-echo Markov process for combinatorial optimization
papers.abstract: We introduce a quantum-echo Markov process for combinatorial optimization. Quantum dynamics based on quantum annealing (QA) or the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) is used to engineer the transition kernel. Increasing the annealing time in QA or the number of layers in QAOA enables transitions to explore distant configurations while suppressing large energy changes. The Hamming-space delocalization originates from operator spreading, whereas the energy-space localization arises from a dynamically generated correlation. For optimization, we propose quantum-echo local optimization. For the ferromagnetic Ising chain, increasing the annealing time or circuit depth yields a nearly quadratic improvement in the dependence of the mean first-passage time on the inverse optimality gap compared with random single-spin flips. For the random Ising model, increasing these parameters initially improves optimization performance, whereas further increases degrade performance in QA and lead to saturation in QAOA. Quantum-echo greedy descent substantially improves the performance, highlighting the complementary roles of quantum dynamics in exploration and greedy descent in exploitation. These results establish quantum-echo dynamics as a framework for engineering structured transition kernels and provide a route to using finite-resource quantum many-body dynamics as a computational primitive for iterative optimization.

papers.title: Server-Side Surrogate Replay for Federated Class-Incremental Learning
papers.abstract: Federated class-incremental learning (FCIL) must learn new classes over time without forgetting the earlier ones. Existing replay methods counter forgetting on the clients, which store exemplars or train on synthetic samples. This burdens resource-constrained clients with extra memory and computation, and since each client stores exemplars only of the classes it has seen, the replay of earlier tasks stays as skewed as its local data. We propose ReSCENE, which moves replay entirely to the server. Each client uploads a few condensed surrogates per class, and the server keeps those of earlier tasks from all clients and trains the global model on them together with the current task, so the replay is balanced across all earlier classes. Since the global model and the surrogates co-evolve within a task, the surrogates of later rounds lie closer to the real data, so we introduce temporal herding, which compresses the pool of each task into a bounded buffer centered on the recent rounds, and establish a condition under which this buffer represents the task data more closely than keeping all surrogates. Across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet, ReSCENE attains the highest average accuracy against eight baselines in all nine settings, by up to $31.1$ points, while requiring as little as $0.11\times$ of the client computation and up to $179\times$ less upload than the model-update baselines. ReSCENE stays ahead with more clients and larger models while keeping client cost low.

papers.title: Exploring the Hidden Cost of the World Around AI Agents
papers.abstract: Agent benchmarks test what agents can do in environments that are built for their tasks. Deployed agents work in the real world where other people and tools can change the state. An agent booking a flight may receive a message from someone else to change the destination, or a booking tool may fail without saying whether the ticket was purchased. We present BACKDROP, which asks how much of an agent's capability in a clean world survives in a non-cooperative world. BACKDROP takes a task along with the agent's execution environment, and plants four everyday hazards in its environment, one at a time and all together. Each hazard tests a different behavior. Authority: does a non-author actor instruction, from anyone who did not author the task, override the user's goal? Injection: does text planted in a record redirect the agent? Boundary: does the agent make changes in an app the user's task did not require? Fault: after a write fails without saying whether it landed, does the agent check before it retries? Across 3,678 variants and 16 models, the average pass rate falls from 69.5% to 31.3% once all four hazards are present; the strongest models fall furthest (Claude Fable 5.1 from 96.6% to 56.0%). The gap is consistent throughout all 16 models. BACKDROP formalizes these gaps and shows how an agent's score in a task's world is a ceiling on real-world performance.

papers.title: Learning via Self-Consistency for Diffusion-based Video Reasoning
papers.abstract: While video diffusion models have demonstrated emerging zero-shot capability for visual reasoning and perception tasks, their stochastic generations often produce inconsistent predictions for tasks requiring reliable, structured outputs. Prior work has shown that self-consistency across stochastic video generations can improve diffusion-based reasoning at test time. We systematically extend the test-time method to structured prediction problems such as referring segmentation. However, test time scaling via self-consistency requires multiple rollouts and incurs much more latency. We propose self-consistency as an intrinsic learning signal for post-training video diffusion models without ground truth annotations or external verifiers. Specifically, our proposed Self-Consistency Fine-Tuning (SC-FT) distills consensus predictions into the video generation model, while subsequent Self-Consistency Reinforcement Learning (SC-RL) rewards generations according to their agreement with the consensus. The resulting model effectively internalizes the benefit of multi-sample consensus and requires only a single generation at inference time, while substantially outperforming the original model. To further reduce inference overhead, we read out predictions early in the denoising trajectory, preserving consensus quality while cutting inference time per rollout by 52%. For visual search, our method raises task accuracy from 48.4% for a single generation to 99.1%. For maze solving across three layout sizes, SC-FT and SC-RL improve single generation strict validity from 59.1% to 66.1% and 95.6% with the same inference latency. Also, for referring segmentation, SC-RL raises single-generation gIoU from 0.402 to 0.582, beyond SC-FT 0.473.

papers.title: When Hedging Changes the Payoff: Option Replication with Price Impact and Execution Costs
papers.abstract: Hedging a derivative by trading the underlying asset changes the payoff that the hedging intended to replicate. We study this phenomenon when trading generates price impact and execution costs. In a binomial model, we characterize replication through a fixed point equation. In continuous time, we derive a nonlinear pricing PDE whose implicit terminal condition captures the nature of the moving target problem of the hedger. For monotone convex Lipschitz payoffs (such as calls and puts) we establish exact replication under midpoint execution costs. Numerical experiments illustrate: (i) how price impact shifts the effective strike, (ii) the nonlinear dependence of the option price on the number of contracts, (iii) how execution costs smooth terminal holdings, (iv) the extent to which the hedger's own trading can bring an otherwise worthless option into the money, and (v) how the spread and the shape of the limit order book in the options market arise from the price impact and the shape of the limit order book of the underlying. In particular, calibrating the one-period binomial model to trade and quote data on near-expiry SPY call options, we find that our model explains 85\% of the observed option bid-ask spread for near-the-money options.

papers.title: Using the Whole Slice: AlphaFold2 Inference on an Eight-Chip TPU v5e
papers.abstract: AlphaFold2 is written in JAX. JAX treats each chip of a tensor processing unit (TPU) slice as a separate device. A JAX program does not spread its work over the chips by itself, so a user who runs AlphaFold2 on a slice can pay for chips that do nothing. We found no published measurement of how AlphaFold2 inference uses a multi-chip TPU slice. Our goal was to measure how much of an eight-chip TPU v5e slice AlphaFold2 inference uses, and which way of mapping the work in JAX uses all of it. Across 12 experiments, the model used random weights, so we studied execution, not prediction quality. By default, only one chip held data. Batching up to eight input sequences (queries) of 118 residues on one chip with JAX's vmap did not raise throughput. Mapping independent queries to the chips with JAX's pmap ran them in parallel on all eight chips. On a grid of 1 to 8 chips and 100 to 1000 residues, eight chips gave 6.5 to 7.9 times the throughput of one chip. JAX's automatic partitioning did not shorten the call for one query. Our program did not tell the partitioner how to split any array across the chips.

papers.title: Anomalous Hardening of a Fluctuation-Induced Gap
papers.abstract: In a mean-field picture, a gap opened by quantum fluctuations grows with them. This can fail if the fluctuating mode is critical and its displacement compensates its coupling to the degenerate states. A single parameter sets the gap response: above a universal threshold, the gap hardens as the critical fluctuations weaken. Whenever the parameter is nonzero, overcompensation beyond the critical point drives a secondary phase transition. In a quantum Rabi ring with synthetic flux, exact diagonalization shows the gap of a photonic Landau level rising by 15% as the critical variance falls by 25%.

papers.title: Surface-Normal Electric Spin in Obliquely Excited Parallel-Slit SPP Fields
papers.abstract: Handedness-dependent light-matter interactions require control of local electric-field rotation, but generating controlled surface-normal spin textures is difficult under oblique illumination. Here, we show that oblique s-polarized illumination of a periodic array of parallel slits produces spatially alternating surface-normal electric spin, with its period tunable by the incidence angle. We further show that the spin texture changes qualitatively between substrate- and air-side excitation depending on whether the SPP field interferes with the excitation field. Under substrate-side excitation, the spin distribution follows the conventional spin-flow relation, whereas under air-side excitation, interference between the SPP and excitation fields produces a distinct spatial periodicity and allows the spin extrema to coincide with the field-intensity maxima. A simple interference model reproduces these contrasting spin textures.

papers.title: An adaptive $L_2$-type test for high-dimensional white noise
papers.abstract: We propose a new $L_2$-type test for white noise which allows the dimension $p$ of the time series to either (i) be a fixed constant, or (ii) diverge with the sample size $n$. The proposed test statistic exhibits an interesting phase transition, following two different regimes of behavior: $p$ is fixed, and $p\rightarrow\infty$. Because identification of the operable regime is difficult, if not impossible in practice, we devise a novel adaptive bootstrap method to construct a unified testing procedure across different phases. Numerical experiments confirm the good finite sample performance of the proposed adaptive $L_2$-type test in comparison to the existing methods in the literature. The proposed testing procedure has been implemented in R package HDTSA.

papers.title: Resolving State-Representation Mismatch: State-Space Visual Reasoning for Open-Loop VLA Planning
papers.abstract: Despite rapid progress in vision-language-action (VLA) models, existing reasoning paradigms still face a fundamental \emph{state-representation mismatch} in open-loop planning. Given only an initial observation, models must internally simulate action-conditioned state transitions, whereas text-, pixel-, and latent-space reasoning can suffer from lossy spatial compression, error-accumulating visual generation, and bypass of intermediate latent tokens, respectively, undermining reliable long-horizon planning. We propose \textbf{State-Space Visual Reasoning} (SSVR), which decouples static visual context, language constraints, and a recurrent latent state. SSVR encodes the initial image and instruction once, then conditions each action prediction on the latent state and updates it with an action-conditioned GRU. Using Qwen2.5-VL as the backbone, SSVR achieves 99.5/99.6, 96.3/98.0, and 83.9/90.6 EM/PR on FrozenLake, Maze, and MiniBehavior, substantially outperforming prior methods. Extensive experiments support the effectiveness of recurrent state modeling for VLA open-loop planning across input transformations and transfer settings. By reusing static visual-textual context and updating a compact recurrent state, SSVR supports efficient multi-step inference, achieving up to $98.58\times$ faster Maze decoding rollouts than the evaluated baselines with the prefix cache prebuilt.

papers.title: On the Complexity of Forcing and Anti-Forcing Minimum Cuts
papers.abstract: For an instance of a combinatorial optimization problem, a \emph{forcing set} is a set of elements such that there is a unique optimal solution including it. Symmetrically, an \emph{anti-forcing set} is a set of elements such that there is a unique optimal solution excluding it. In this paper, we study the problems of computing smallest forcing and anti-forcing sets for two classical cut problems, \textsc{Global Min Cut} and \textsc{Min $s$--$t$ Cut}. We also consider variants in which the optimal cut to be uniquely determined is given as input. For each of these problems, we either give a polynomial-time algorithm or prove \NP-completeness.

papers.title: $\textit{Nāpōwawā`enakaulua}$: a close quasar pair at cosmic dawn in the Aether survey
papers.abstract: We present the discovery and first characterization of $\textit{Nāpōwawā`enakaulua}$: the most compact known quasar pair candidate in the Epoch of Reionization, with a projected separation of only $0.98^{\prime\prime}$ ($\approx 5.56$ pkpc at $z \sim 6.08$) and a velocity offset of $Δv \simeq 15 \text{ km s}^{-1}$. Using spectroscopy from JWST/NIRSpec integral field unit, as part of the $\textit{Aether survey}$, Gemini/GNIRS and GMOS we characterize the continuum and emission line properties of the two quasars, enabling constraints on their black hole masses ($M_{\text{BH}} \simeq 1.5 \times 10^9$ and $4.0 \times 10^8\,M_\odot$), accretion states ($λ_{\text{Edd}} \simeq 1.23$ and $1.07$), and systemic redshifts ($z_{\rm sys} \simeq 6.0781$ and $6.0785$). We place this pair in the cosmological context by comparing the chance of occurrence to extrapolations of high-$z$ quasar clustering measurements at larger scales, resulting in a $\sim 2-3$ order of magnitude excess with respect to expectations. This excess hints at an underlying population of merger-triggered quasar pairs at cosmic dawn or to a denser-than-average galactic environment. $\textit{Nāpōwawā`enakaulua}$ thus represents a crucial signpost to investigate the mass assembly of the first massive galaxies and black holes.

papers.title: Non-vanishing of the structure-sheaf cohomology of affine henselian schemes and henselian affinoids
papers.abstract: Let $(A,I)$ be a henselian pair such that $A$ is a domain of characteristic zero and $I\ne0$. We prove that any flat affine henselian scheme of finite presentation over $(A,I)$ has nonzero first structure-sheaf cohomology whenever one of its fibers over a point in $V(I)$ has positive dimension. This in particular gives a negative answer to the question by Devadas in the mixed-characteristic case. As an application, we also prove that the first structure-sheaf cohomology does not vanish for henselian affinoids of positive dimensions.

papers.title: Robo-Harness K1: Harnessing Robot-Use Agents via Perception Augmentation
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) understand manipulation scenes and instructions, yet as robot-use agents they struggle to turn 2D observations into the 3D relations that motion requires. We introduce Robo-Harness K1, a robot-use agent harness built on perception as tools. K1 offers region grounding, calibrated depth and geometry, persistent visual anchors, and projected grasp candidates as callable tools. The VLM calls them to measure the scene, chooses its next motion from the results, and measures again after it acts. On LIBERO-PRO, K1 raises Gemini 3.7 Flash from 16.7% to 71.7% and GPT-6 Astra from 63.3% to 93.3%, with the largest gains on spatial tasks. Without fine-tuning, the Gemini agent transfers to three RoboSuite arms, dual-arm RoboTwin tasks, and mobile manipulation in RoboCasa. In real-world experiments on a Piper arm, K1 completes eight of nine concluded trials across three tasks. Agentic post-training further distills a frontier model's traces into a compact agent: trained on 107 successful episodes, Qwen3.5-9B reaches 44.2% on new initial states and 13.9% on held-out task conditions, versus 30.2% and 0.0% for OpenVLA trained on the same episodes. Mixed training on traces from four environments raises held-out accuracy from 11.1% to 27.8% and RoboSuite success from 28.3% to 50.0%. These results support perceptual tool use for deploying and training robot-use agents.

papers.title: How Attackers Launder Funds through Mixers: Characterization and Detection on Ethereum
papers.abstract: Mixers protect privacy by concealing deposit--withdrawal links, but are also abused to launder illicit funds. Existing anti-money laundering studies do not specifically target mixer laundering, while mixer research focuses on deanonymization rather than identifying laundering-related transactions. Public reports remain fragmented, leaving no public case-level dataset for systematic measurement and detection. To fill this void, this paper presents the first comprehensive study of mixer laundering on Ethereum. We first construct \textsc{MixLaunder}, the first public case-level dataset of mixer laundering. It covers 27 cases involving Tornado Cash and Railgun from 2020 to 2025 and labels 9,300 laundering-related transactions with case identities and observable upstream and downstream fund flows, including deposits totaling approximately \$1.1 billion. By comparing these transactions with background mixer usage, we identify five common strategies, showing that laundering evidence spans complementary behavioral and fund-flow contexts, while same-case activity is locally tight but weakly connected across bursts. Our analysis further reveals coverage gaps in mixer-side risk screening and representative deanonymization heuristics. Guided by these findings, we develop \textsc{MixGuard}, which combines tri-view representation learning with two-stage grouping for transaction-level detection and case-aware grouping. Under strict case-level holdout evaluation, \textsc{MixGuard} outperforms representative baselines, achieving 97.89\% detection precision and 98.73\% group purity, while its top ten groups cover 95.09\% of each case's transactions on average.

papers.title: Can We Predict kNN-Based Anomalous Sound Detection Performance from Embedding-Space Geometry?
papers.abstract: Anomaly detection systems are often trained using normal data alone, while model selection and evaluation typically require labeled anomalies. We study anomaly-free selection for k-nearest neighbor (kNN)-based anomaly detectors operating on embedding spaces, using pretrained audio representations and temporal pooling for first-shot industrial anomalous sound detection as a practically relevant application. We derive a lower bound on the area under the ROC curve (AUC) at the score level and use it to analyze kNN-based detection, relating score variability to the geometry of the embedding space. Under a local scaling model, we characterize how density variation, intrinsic-dimensional heterogeneity, and cross-domain mismatch contribute to inlier-score variability, and show how local density-based score normalization (LDN) affects these contributions. We then investigate anomaly-free model selection and show that inlier score variance alone does not reliably predict performance across different representations. To address this limitation, we introduce simple pseudo-anomaly probes that provide a reference for estimating relative score separation. Experiments on the DCASE 2022-2025 benchmarks, spanning four pretrained audio encoders and 208 candidate systems evaluate both kNN and LDN. The results show that LDN improves detection performance, while pseudo-anomaly-based estimators substantially improve anomaly-free model selection. The AUC Bound provides robust selection across pseudo-anomaly constructions, and a simple metadata-free construction offers a competitive alternative to existing approaches, even outperforming conventional development-set selection when combined with LDN.

papers.title: Decoupling Logical Masks from GPU Execution for Dynamic Block-Sparse Attention
papers.abstract: Attention computation makes inference expensive in video diffusion transformers (vDiTs), which generate videos through iterative denoising. Block-sparse attention (BSA) reduces this cost by computing only blocks selected by a logical mask, which specifies the attention interactions to compute. Existing BSA runtimes either fix one physical execution plan per block geometry, which limits adaptation to varying masks and graphics processing units (GPUs), or plan each mask at runtime, which adds preparation overhead to every request. Because masks change across requests, this per-mask planning must be repeated, so its cost can outweigh the execution-time savings. We present Tessera, a runtime for dynamic BSA that decouples logical masks from GPU execution through two-layer physical execution plans that preserve the specified attention interactions. First, its physical mapping layer retains, combines, or subdivides logical blocks into physical tiles suited to different mask shapes and GPU architectures. Second, its task organization layer groups and schedules tiles within GPU tasks to reuse data, expose parallelism, and overlap data movement with computation. Third, its plan selector chooses a plan for each request with low overhead, through either a plan table built from offline profiling or a calibrated cost model, which extends selection to masks outside the profiled distribution and to a new GPU with about 100 calibration requests. Implemented with specialized CUDA kernels for four NVIDIA GPU generations and evaluated on 2,312 real attention masks and two video diffusion models, Tessera achieves up to $2.88\times$ BSA request speedup over baseline systems in these models and speeds up their 50-step loop by $1.21$--$1.24\times$.

papers.title: Metric-Bench: Exploring In-context Spatial Metric Reasoning in VLMs for Indoor Scenes
papers.abstract: Metric reasoning is a critical and challenging task for Vision Language Models (VLMs), playing a pivotal role in embodied AI tasks such as robotic manipulation and autonomous navigation. However, current spatial reasoning remains bottlenecked by rigid pixel-level supervision; such localized optimization often compromises general multimodal intelligence, triggering performance degradation or catastrophic forgetting of broad reasoning capabilities. To address these limitations, we introduce Metric-Bench, a focused benchmark designed to guide metric-spatial reasoning using contextual information. By incorporating in-image reference objects with known physical dimensions, Metric-Bench guides models to implicitly learn the 2D-to-3D mapping without camera intrinsics. We further present MetricReasoner, a task-adapted reinforcement fine-tuning recipe for reference-grounded metric reasoning, using structured prompts and verifiable numerical rewards. Extensive experiments on Metric-Bench demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances spatial metric understanding, outperforming existing and even larger proprietary models by 43.1\%, while improving downstream embodied performance over a spatial-specialized counterpart by 30.4\% on RoboSpatial overall accuracy and 9.3\% on ERQA, and additionally delivering consistent gains on general benchmarks (15.9\% on V$\star$Bench, 88.9\% on BLINK), indicating that the proposed adaptation does not necessarily compromise general VLM capabilities.

papers.title: Lattice in Line: Optimized DMRG ordering for complex lattice geometries
papers.abstract: The density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) is a one-dimensional tensor-network technique, but it is not limited to one-dimensional systems: it can be applied to periodic 2D and 3D clusters and molecules, provided their sites are first enumerated along a line; a step one may call ``lattice compilation''. This paper discusses three proxy loss functions for finding this optimal enumeration: the graph bandwidth $B$ (maximum interaction range), the cutwidth $C$ (maximum number of bonds crossing a cut), and the average interaction range $R$. Constructing the Hamiltonian MPO (matrix-product operator) for a large set of clusters that are of interest in frustrated magnetism, I find that $C$ determines the peak SU(2) Heisenberg MPO bond dimension and $R$ the average one. Targeting $(C,R)$ lexicographically yields the best energies. Targeting $B$ indirectly reduces $C$, but not as efficiently as targeting $C$ directly. Otherwise, the value of $B$ itself is largely irrelevant in the sense that good DMRG energies can have large $B$. To perform the optimization, classic heuristics (e.g.\ reverse Cuthill--McKee) prove unreliable even for small clusters, and I find that a QUBO formulation improves them only marginally. Instead I propose a staged optimization built on Boolean satisfiability (SAT) and constraint-programming (CP) solvers, CP-SAT of Google's OR-Tools (a hybrid of CP propagation and SAT clause learning) and the SAT solvers CaDiCaL and Glucose. This approach yields significantly better orderings together with rigorous bounds. The corresponding \textit{Lattice in Line} code is available at https://github.com/spinflip/lattice_in_line and was designed with extensive use of the Fable 5 large language model.

papers.title: Universal $Z^{2/3}/\sqrt{Q_α}$ Scaling Law in Alpha Decay from Nuclei to Neutron-Star Mergers
papers.abstract: We establish a universal scaling law for $α$-decay half-lives based on the variable $X_a = Z^a/\sqrt{Q_α}$, which collapses experimental and theoretical data spanning over twenty orders of magnitude onto a single linear correlation. Global optimization over the complete set of even-even $α$ emitters reveals a uniquely sharp optimum at $a \simeq 2/3$. This exponent is theoretically motivated by the leading geometric scaling of heavy nuclei and emerges quantitatively from the correlated nuclear systematics, driven by the correlated $(Z, Q_α)$ manifold of the nuclear chart. Strikingly, five structurally distinct semi-empirical models and an independent microscopic WKB calculation, when independently optimized with respect to the exponent $a$, yield values clustered around $2/3$, while the corresponding $a=2/3$ correlations remain highly linear without refitting the original model parameters. This emergent scaling law implies smooth variations of decay times along the heavy $r$-process path. We demonstrate analytically that, given a roughly uniform distribution of this variable, the scaling law naturally supports a quasi-power-law radioactive heating rate ($\dotε \propto t^{-1.24}$), consistent with full network calculations. Furthermore, integrating these scaling predictions directly into nuclear source terms for radiative-diffusion models yields multimessenger observables that accurately reproduce the kilonova AT2017gfo associated with the gravitational-wave event GW170817, demonstrating that the $Z^{2/3}/\sqrt{Q_α}$ scaling coordinate provides a robust tool for modeling the radioactive engines of neutron-star mergers.

papers.title: Jev for Scientific Decisions: Evaluating Semantic Choices and Their Consequences
papers.abstract: Scientific workflows often require choosing among known relations before a deterministic calculation can proceed. Whether observations share a culture, treatment or reference standard can change the scientific meaning of the resulting count or comparison. Once the evidence is prepared and the calculation is written as code, this decision reduces to selecting one of the listed candidates. We evaluate Jev on this step, using a harness that follows its documented guidance. The study compares twelve model configurations on ten scientific cases built from published sources. Each case contains two Choices, which are questions with listed candidates. Each case is repeated five times per configuration. We measure selections, downstream outputs and final labels separately. Jev tied with five other configurations at complete semantic correctness and achieved the lowest median latency and mean cost. On one Choice, whether samples came from one culture, three comparison configurations made seven wrong selections that changed downstream counts while preserving the correct final label. These results support using Jev to select relations when the evidence and candidates are prepared in advance. They also show that evaluating it requires checking the selections and downstream outputs that a workflow will reuse.

papers.title: Few-Shot Demonstrations Elicit the Use of In-Context World Representations in LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), when acting as agents, are expected to take observed data in context, infer the latent state space underlying the world, and leverage it for downstream prediction. However, prior work demonstrated that LLMs struggle to use representations learned in context on a graph tracking task, where the model needs to construct a representation of the graph governing data generation process and use it for subsequent predictions. In this paper, we show that extending this to few-shot settings, where each demonstration is generated from a different world with either the same or different graph topologies, enhances its prediction on 9 models from 7 model families. To understand this improvement, we linearly probe a low-dimensional world representation that encodes graph information in the hidden states. Notably, we find that few-shot demonstrations relocate the world representation and increase its predictive use. Specifically, for each model, these world representations shift in directions nearly orthogonal to their original subspace, and interventions on these representations selectively impair performance more than interventions on other subspaces. Consistent with this insight, we show that few-shot demonstrations with observations from different worlds improve performance on ARC-AGI-1&2, web agent tasks, and Othello. Our findings elucidate the role and internal mechanisms of few-shot demonstrations in in-context world modeling and provide implications for their further improvement.

papers.title: BabelArena: A Large-Scale Multilingual Benchmark for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly execute multi-step workflows through tool use and interaction with users and environments. However, current agent evaluations are largely English-centric, limiting our understanding of agent capabilities in multilingual settings. We introduce BabelFlow, a benchmark-general agentic workflow that adapts existing agent benchmarks to new languages by analyzing runtime dependencies, coordinating structure-preserving translation, and combining multi-layer verification with human review to preserve task and evaluation semantics. Using BabelFlow, we construct BabelArena, a task-aligned benchmark comprising 16,146 instances derived from 702 canonical tasks across four benchmark families, 13 domains, and 23 languages. Experiments with five frontier models show that no single model dominates across benchmark families and that cross-language disparities extend well beyond task success. Lower-resource languages exhibit distinct failure patterns, with larger shares of tool-use and control-flow errors rather than answer-quality errors alone, pointing to gaps in reliable task execution across the resource levels of these languages. On the same tasks, agents in low-resource languages also consume substantially more tokens than in English (up to roughly twice the input) without proportional increases in interaction length, and language consistency degrades further on tasks requiring structured output, where switches are directed overwhelmingly toward English. We believe BabelArena provides a foundation for advancing research on reliable and efficient multilingual agents.

papers.title: RLVR$^{2}$: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rubric-based Ranking
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is expanding from tasks with well-defined correctness signals, such as mathematics and code, toward multifaceted quality requirements specified by multi-dimensional rubrics. Since policy optimization consumes one scalar per rollout, rubric-based pipelines must map multiple criterion scores into a scalar reward. This aggregation is often treated as score scaling, but it implicitly determines how quality dimensions trade off during training. The prevailing practice, normalizing each criterion and taking a linear combination, assumes that cardinal score differences are comparable across criteria and that gains on one criterion compensate for failures on another; both assumptions are unreliable when criteria are semantically heterogeneous. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rubric-based Ranking (RLVR$^2$), a verifiable ranking paradigm for rubric-based RLVR. For each criterion, RLVR$^2$ converts rubric scores into criterion-specific within-group ordinal outcomes, recovers a latent utility from the resulting comparison matrix, and merges these utilities into one training signal. By retaining only within-group ordering and discarding raw score magnitudes, RLVR$^2$ avoids calibrating heterogeneous rubric scales. It further supports objective-preserving attribute adjustment: auxiliary attributes that correlate with observed rankings but are not training objectives can enter the estimation without expanding the rubric or rewarding them directly. Across three model scales and 16 benchmarks, RLVR$^2$ consistently outperforms representative rubric-based baselines, achieving the best overall performance on most benchmarks at every scale. Analysis shows it controls systematic effects tied to reasoning efficiency and response formatting while preserving the quality objective.

papers.title: Mixture Density Networks for Neutrino Reconstruction at Hadron Colliders
papers.abstract: Neutrino momentum reconstruction at hadron colliders is intrinsically ambiguous because the longitudinal momentum is not directly observed. We study this problem in semileptonic $t\bar{t}$ events using \monster{} (Mixture of Neutrino Solutions with Transformer Event Representation), a mixture density network that predicts a multivariate normal mixture for the conditional distribution of neutrino momentum from reconstructed event objects. The model uses a Transformer-based event encoder and yields a sampling-free point estimate of the neutrino momentum from the closed-form density. On the public benchmark introduced with \nuflows, \monster{} reduces the 68th percentile of the three-momentum residual by 5\% and the 95th percentile by 6\% relative to the empirical-mode \nuflows{} baseline, with per-variable root-mean-square errors smaller by 2 to 9\% at comparable bias, while running 2 to 8.5 times faster at inference, depending on the device and batch size. These results indicate that mixture density networks are a competitive alternative to normalizing flows for neutrino reconstruction.

papers.title: ConsistWorld: Evidence Routing for Consistent Multi-Agent World Models
papers.abstract: Autoregressive video world models enable temporally coherent generation for a single observer. Extending them to multiple agents requires consistency across independently controlled views and temporal gaps under causal streaming. We present ConsistWorld, a multi-agent world model that generates camera-controlled video streams of a static scene from one shared image. We formulate consistency as routing evidence from committed multi-agent history and concurrently generated peer views to the tokens being generated. Pose Conditioned Memory Retrieval selects relevant historical observations from all agents, recovering evidence beyond the recent context window. Visibility-Gated Peer Sharing regulates current peer information according to estimated historical coverage and current-view overlap. Together, they determine which historical observations enter the context and where concurrent peer information contributes, supporting long-term recall and coordinated exploration. Both mechanisms use camera geometry and maintain a bounded active context for a fixed agent count and retrieval budget. Experiments on evidence sharing cases and video length and agent number generalizations show that ConsistWorld achieves a strong cross-time and cross-agent consistency while preserving competitive generation quality.

papers.title: Outpainting: spatially extending aero-optic phase screens
papers.abstract: Aero-optic effects distort light wave propagation near a high-speed aircraft, thereby degrading performance in airborne imaging and communication systems. Measuring aero-optic data through experiment is costly and the resulting data often has a limited spatial size. Further, alternative methods for simulating this data, including computational fluid dynamics and conventional phase screen generation algorithms (e.g., boiling flow), face drawbacks such as large computation time or inaccurate statistics. More recently, data-driven algorithms have been proposed that can synthesize data that matches relevant statistics of measured aero-optic data. However, these methods cannot spatially extend aero-optic data. In this paper, we introduce ReVAR-ext (Re-whitened Vector AutoRegression-extender), an algorithm that builds on an existing data-driven approach, ReVAR, to spatially extend measured aero-optic data (a process called outpainting) and match the spatial and temporal correlations of the measured data. ReVAR-ext generalizes the generation process of ReVAR by combining multiple sets of synthetic data with the input measured data. This approach generates multiple fixed-sized synthetic images, each of which overlaps with the input data, and then stitches them together. When paired with ReVAR, the ReVAR-ext algorithm can generate aero-optic data with arbitrary temporal duration and arbitrary spatial size. Our experiments show that extended data generated by ReVAR-ext closely matches the temporal power spectrum of two measured aero-optic data sets. Further, the extended data approximately matches the spatial autocorrelation, with reduced accuracy at large spatial lags and at vertical lags.

papers.title: Designer-RSI: Evolving Procedural Memory from User Traffic for Graphic Design Agent
papers.abstract: Deployed software agents face a continuous stream of user requests while their foundation-model weights remain frozen between releases. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) via external memory offers a practical path to continual adaptation, yet prior methods largely assume programmatic verifiers, cheap retries, or a single global prompt. Creative software breaks these assumptions, as open-ended visual briefs lack ground truth, VLM judges are noisy, and multi-step tool executions are costly and confounded by external assets. We present Designer-RSI, which evolves a modular skill bank from unlabeled design trajectories for an agent spanning over 230 raster, vector, and layout tools. Designer-RSI couples widening (acquiring new skills for recurring capability gaps) with deepening (revising failing skills by contrasting successful and failed runs), and screens updates through a Pareto-style matched replay gate that requires strict gains on sampled briefs without local regressions. Across held-out product briefs, eight external benchmarks, and two backbones, traffic-driven evolution outperforms static documentation skills, lifts execution success up to 99.8%, improves requirement fulfillment, and reaches up to a 67.6% blind win rate over the base agent. Ablations further show that skill acquisition and revision are strongly synergistic: neither suffices alone, and reliable gains require evolving coverage and execution quality together.

papers.title: SWE-Proof: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World Issues with Machine-Checked Proofs?
papers.abstract: Ensuring the correctness of LLM-generated code is a core challenge for modern software engineering. Benchmarks for agentic code generation check correctness with held-out test suites, which are inherently incomplete and increasingly susceptible to memorization. Formal verification avoids both problems, but existing work covers only standalone tasks whose specifications are given as input, not real issues, which touch large repositories and state intent in vague natural language. We present BenchProofer, a pipeline that turns a coding task with a known correct patch into a formally verified one: it writes a specification for the new code, summarizes the existing functions that code calls with axioms, and admits an instance only after mechanical and adversarial gates agree. Applying it to SWE-bench Verified yields SWE-Proof, 500 real issues whose correctness is formally verified rather than tested, and it extends to SWE-bench Pro. Evaluating Claude Opus 4.8, we find that verification catches what tests miss: nearly a third of test-passing patches admit counterexamples, which a structured natural-language specification does not fix, while a correct formal one lifts resolution from 85% to 95%. Writing that specification is the hard part: an agent that must write its own gains nothing over an unaided baseline, and only 56% of those specifications pass our audit. The usual failure is faithfulness, where a specification constrains part of the required behavior and leaves the rest free. Specification quality also tracks the outcome, failing on 92% of unresolved instances against 51% of resolved ones, making faithful specification synthesis a concrete open problem. Code is available at https://github.com/amazon-science/BenchProofer.

papers.title: Binary Minor Certificates for the $\mathcal A(1)$-hit problem of $MO(2)$
papers.abstract: Let $M=\widetilde H^*(MO(2);\mathbb F_2)$ and let $\mathcal A(1)$ be the subalgebra of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra generated by $\operatorname{Sq}^1$ and $\operatorname{Sq}^2$. In this work, we determine the quotient $\mathbb F_2\otimes_{\mathcal A(1)}M$ in every internal degree $h\geq0$, where internal degree $h$ corresponds to cohomological degree $h+2$. To overcome the limitations of finite experimental extrapolation, our proof is strictly certifying: in each degree, we exhibit a determinant-one minor of the binary hit matrix and a complementary family of linear dual functionals annihilating every hit column, mathematically guaranteeing the exact rank for all degrees. This rigorously establishes the monomial generating families and module decomposition proposed in Shih's 2012 report. Furthermore, we derive a closed binomial formula for every Steenrod square from the length-two symmetric-polynomial model, correct a boundary omission in the $\mathcal A(0)$ calculation, compute the exact Hilbert series of the $\mathcal A(1)$-cohit, and prove an intrinsic direct-sum decomposition of $M$ into two stable $\mathcal A(1)$-submodules.

papers.title: PointEvent: Polarity-Conditioned Motion Evidence Accumulation for Event-Based Tiny Object Detection
papers.abstract: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and motion sensitivity for tiny UAV detection, but distant targets produce sparse, fragmented events easily overwhelmed by clutter and noise. Dense aggregation mixes weak target responses with background activity, while local spatiotemporal modeling may fail to connect distant observations. Polarity encodes the sign of brightness change; a moving target tends to produce opposite polarities at its leading and trailing boundaries, whose spatial arrangement indicates motion direction. We propose PointEvent, which serializes events into complementary spatiotemporal and timestamp orders. Spatiotemporal orders preserve x-y-t locality, while timestamp orders preserve temporal succession across spatial neighborhoods, establishing long-range propagation paths. Along each path, a recurrent state accumulates evidence, while polarity routes each event to its corresponding state subspace. This separates how evidence propagates from where it is written. Experiments on EV-UAV and ES-UAV demonstrate state-of-the-art accuracy with the fewest parameters (0.12M) and fastest measured inference (29.9 ms) among compared methods. Code: https://github.com/wzz-z/PointEvent

papers.title: Graph-Based Stochastic Power-UCT: Monte-Carlo Graph Search with Power Mean Estimation
papers.abstract: Tree-based Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) duplicates the same state when it is reached through different trajectories, which can waste simulations in stochastic MDPs. We introduce Graph-Based Stochastic-Power-UCT (GS-Power-UCT), which shares states reached at the same planning depth while keeping separate values for states reached at different depths. This design applies to general stochastic MDPs, including problems with cycles. We prove that for a fixed planning horizon, the root estimate converges to the finite-horizon value at rate $O(n^{-1/2})$, matching tree-based Stochastic-Power-UCT while reusing samples across shared states. We also study two full-state variants: GS-Power-UCT-F, which stores one node per physical state to increase sample sharing but may mix values from different remaining horizons, and GS-Power-UCT-F$^+$, which uses an adaptive horizon to control this bias. The latter converges to $V^{\star}(s_0)$, the optimal infinite-horizon discounted value at the root state $s_0$, when the remaining cross-depth gap vanishes. Experiments on stochastic planning benchmarks show improved sample efficiency over tree-based and graph-based baselines.

papers.title: Contact Large Deviations of Stochastic Vector Bundles
papers.abstract: A dissipative system distributes over its state space, and its rare events are measured on an exponential scale by a rate function. This paper shows that one contact form carries both. On the bundle of jets of probability densities over the state space, the constraint function of the contact potential is a first integral of the characteristic field, so the action is affine in the elapsed time along each characteristic and the contact probability measure of a Lagrangian section has that action as its exponent at every finite time, with no path integral, no variational problem over curves and no coercivity hypothesis. The rate function is the deficit of the action below its supremum, and is therefore a transported conserved quantity rather than the value of a limit; its amplitude is invariant and its non-degeneracy is decided by the initial section alone. Large deviations form the concentration regime of this finite-time structure and require one condition, the smooth convergence of the endpoint map of the characteristic flow to a diffeomorphism. The drift and the fluctuation tensor are the first two coefficients of the same potential, the second confined to the iso-density surfaces by the degeneracy condition, so the fluctuation is constrained by the invariant density rather than chosen beside the drift. The entropy production is an observable of the same measure, and a fibre involution yields a Gallavotti--Cohen-type duality between the forward and the reversed ensembles under a separation condition on the tilted action.

papers.title: Ancilla-assisted multi-qubit quantum gates with polar molecules
papers.abstract: Quantum error correction enables reliable quantum computation using imperfect physical gates, but its implementation often requires multi-qubit controlled-unitary gates $\text{C}_{\mathbb{N}}(U)$ acting on $\mathbb{N} \ge 3$ qubits. Their direct realization is challenging, while decomposing them into standard one-qubit and two-qubit gates can increase circuit depth and error rates. Here, we present an ancilla-assisted scheme to directly implement $\text{C}_{\mathbb{N}}(U)$ in optically trapped ultracold polar molecules. By appropriately selecting qubit states for the ancilla and data qubits, dark states can appear during two smooth $π$ pulses. This can generate a controlled-phase gate with the phase set by the relative phase between the pulses; notably, a single $2π$ pulse yields a $\text{C}_{\mathbb{N}}(Z)$ gate. Numerical analysis for a simple molecular spatial configuration demonstrates that the gate infidelity is dominated by qubit decoherence, yielding a $\text{C}_2(Z)$ fidelity of $0.996$ estimated with $T_2^\ast=1.5$~s and a gate duration of $T \approx 4\text{~ms}$. Furthermore, diabatic errors remain low, on the order of $10^{-4}$ for $\mathbb{N}=2,3$ and $10^{-3}$ for $\mathbb{N}=4$, even with dipole-dipole interaction strengths as low as $25\hbar/T$.

papers.title: Radiation Magneto-hydrodynamic Simulations of MRI with Zero-Net-Vertical-Flux: Necessity of Resolving the Thermal Scale For Strongly Magnetized Initial Conditions
papers.abstract: We perform 3D radiation magneto-hydrodynamic (RMHD) shearing-box simulations of local patches of optically thick accretion disks, applicable to sub-Eddington active galactic nuclei (AGN) at $\sim 1000$ gravitational radii around a supermassive black hole (SMBH) of $10^7-10^8M_\odot$. In particular, we set up zero-net-vertical-flux (ZNVF) simulations with strong net azimuthal fields ($B_y$) characterized by initial gas-to-magnetic pressure ratio $β_0$. We find that $β_0 \sim 1$ simulations relax to the classical MRI state with steady-state $β\sim 10-20$ and slow periodic reversals of the mean azimuthal field (dynamo cycles), losing memory of their initial $B_y$ configuration. The outcome of simulations starting from $β_0=0.1$ (superthermal magnetic pressures) depends upon the numerical resolution as quantified by the number of grid cells per thermal scale height $H_\mathrm{th}$. Resolved simulations ($Δz\le H_\mathrm{th}/5$) settle into final states similar to the larger-$β_0$ runs, exhibiting thermally dominated midplanes heated by MRI turbulence and undergoing dynamo cycles. In contrast, lower resolution $β_0 = 0.1$ runs evolve towards states dominated by a coherent mean field, similar to what is observed in recent isothermal MHD simulations. However, those disks fail to sustain sufficient turbulent heating near the midplane and undergo runaway cooling and contraction. While such states might be sustained in global models with even lower initial $β_0$ and/or continuous $B_y$ injection, our results indicate that they could arise purely from under-resolving the midplane MRI dynamo that would otherwise be able to generate and emanate randomized fields. We highlight the need to resolve a fraction of the thermal scale height (the classical MRI wavelengths) for strongly magnetized initial conditions to obtain converged outcomes in RMHD simulations.

papers.title: Every integer greater than 24 is the sum of a prime and a non-square-free integer
papers.abstract: Lee and O'Clarey proved that every odd integer $n>24$ can be written as the sum of a prime and a positive integer that is not square-free. Under the generalised Riemann hypothesis, they established the same conclusion for every integer $n>24$. We prove this result unconditionally, confirming their stated expectation. The proof combines an elementary congruence argument, finite computation, and explicit estimates for primes in arithmetic progressions.

papers.title: Modular flow and the area operator
papers.abstract: In the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence, the Jafferis-Lewkowycz-Maldacena-Suh (JLMS) formula relates the boundary modular Hamiltonian to the HRT area operator and the corresponding bulk modular Hamiltonian. In standard discussions of a holographic code built from perturbative excitations on a fixed classical background, the $A/4G$ term dominates over the bulk modular Hamiltonian in the limit $G \to 0$. However, this setup is insufficient to describe the action of boundary modular flows that change the classical background. In contrast, our recent discussion of `large' codes provides a useful framework to obtain a JLMS formula that relates bulk and boundary modular flows acting on appropriate states in the code. Here, one sees that the bulk modular Hamiltonian is not in fact subdominant when the modular flow defined by one state acts on another state peaked around a sufficiently different classical background. Instead, the bulk modular Hamiltonian can be of order $1/G$ and can dominate over the $A/4G$ term. Nevertheless, we show that if the two states have the same classical background except for data conjugate to the HRT area then, under mild assumptions and over a large range of flow parameters, the modular-flowed state is described by a classical background given by the HRT-area flow alone.

papers.title: Fairness Auditing After Model Updating: Reliability of Paired Disparity Comparisons
papers.abstract: Model updates can change disparities in prediction errors between demographic groups. We examine whether retrospective audits can reliably assess these changes by comparing updated models with their unchanged initial models on the same independent labelled observations, holding completed updating histories fixed. The target is the updated-minus-frozen difference in absolute subgroup gaps, averaged equally across reporting periods and assessed separately for true-positive and false-positive rates. Exploratory controlled simulations and repeated audits of fixed simulated histories assess coverage and decision correctness for nominal 95% intervals. Across the broader history panel, changing interval construction can raise or lower estimated coverage. In one subgroup-drift setting, 2,000 true-positive-rate audits evaluated twenty selected histories updated at fixed intervals, using 1,250 observations per reporting period. Replacing percentile bootstrap intervals with full-size basic intervals reduced estimated coverage from 92.20% to 84.55%. At an illustrative margin of 0.5 percentage points, correct conclusive decisions increased from 78 to 376, while incorrect decisions increased from 3 to 43, including 13 false reductions. The constructions used identical observations, estimates and bootstrap draws and had equal widths. Other controlled examples frequently excluded the population change while correctly indicating an increase. More conclusive audit results therefore need not provide more reliable evidence. Claims that updating reduced disparity require an inference procedure justified for the target and sampling design, an explicit decision margin, and group-specific performance reporting.

papers.title: Analytic motions of spinning particles in Schwarzschild-(anti-)de Sitter spacetime
papers.abstract: The motion of a spinning test particle in a static, spherically symmetric spacetime with a cosmological constant is studied within the Mathisson-Papapetrou-Dixon formalism, working to linear order in the particle's spin. By exploiting the symmetries of the background, the radial and latitudinal dynamics are reduced to first-order equations governed by a spin-deformed quintic polynomial. A complete classification of the real root structure of this quintic is carried out, from which the allowed orbital types for spinning particles in the Schwarzschild-anti-de Sitter and Schwarzschild-de Sitter geometries follow directly. The parameter dependence of the root structure and of the stable circular orbit interval is analyzed. In particular, for values of the cosmological constant beyond the Stuchlík limit, where spinless particles admit no bound orbits, spinning particles can still remain bound. The radial motion is expressed piecewise in terms of Lauricella hypergeometric functions, with the simple positive real roots of the quintic acting as branch cuts. The latitudinal motion consists of small oscillations about an equatorial plane, and its phase, governed by the same quintic, admits an analogous analytic representation.

papers.title: Global mild solutions and the semiclassical limit for the Fermi--Dirac BGK model
papers.abstract: We prove global existence of mild solutions to the spatially inhomogeneous Fermi--Dirac BGK equation for arbitrary-size Pauli-admissible initial data with finite mass and kinetic energy, allowing both vacuum and locally saturated zero-temperature states. The construction relies on a moment-compatible regularization of the local equilibrium that preserves the Pauli bound and uniform moment control while remaining consistent up to the saturation boundary. The solutions satisfy mass, momentum, and energy conservation and, under an additional finite spatial second-moment assumption, an entropy-gap H-theorem on the full Pauli interval. Under uniform moment and entropy bounds, we further prove that, after extraction of a subsequence, quantum mild solutions converge strongly in phase space, uniformly on bounded time intervals, to a mild solution of the classical BGK equation.

papers.title: Support Topology and Gradient Mixing in Sinkhorn Layers
papers.abstract: Sinkhorn attention layers normalize weights over a fixed sparse mask by alternating row and column scaling. When training these layers, sparse masks are usually judged by their edge count, graph diameter, or forward reachability. We show that the sparsity pattern and marginal budgets also govern how gradients flow backward through the scaling steps. Differentiating one row-column cycle on column log-potentials yields an explicit row-stochastic Markov kernel built from the two half-step transport plans, which reduces to a reversible two-step random walk at a balanced fixed point. Because potentials are defined only up to additive constants on each connected component, reverse-mode gradients propagate as zero-sum vectors whose total-variation norm contracts at a rate given by the kernel's Dobrushin coefficient. This coefficient bounds both unrolled backpropagation and implicit-differentiation truncation error. Crucially, graph connectivity alone does not prevent gradient trapping: we prove a face-lattice dichotomy showing that a mask and marginals guarantee score-uniform one-step contraction if and only if every nonempty face of the transportation polytope retains pairwise two-hop column overlap; otherwise, large learned scores can push the contraction rate arbitrarily close to one. We extend this criterion to multi-layer schedules, prove exact one-sweep mixing for coordinate-factorized and butterfly masks, and derive closed-form bounds for expanders, local bands, and global hub tokens. Deterministic numerical checks verify our finite-difference adjoints, canonical sparse masks, adversarial score limits, and spectral formulas.

papers.title: Leakage current evolution in LHCb VELO sensors during Run 1-2 LHC data taking period
papers.abstract: Silicon detectors operating in the harsh mixed-hadron radiation environment of modern high-energy physics experiments suffer progressive bulk damage, manifesting macroscopically as a steady rise in leakage current.

papers.title: Constrained Online Learning with Noisy Constraint Values
papers.abstract: We study online convex optimization with time-varying constraints when the constraint values are observed only through noise. In each round the learner picks an action, pays a convex loss, and incurs a convex constraint value that should be nonpositive; it then receives unbiased estimates of the loss and constraint gradients, and an unbiased observation of the constraint value whose error has bounded variance. Performance is measured against the best fixed action in hindsight among those that satisfy every constraint, and violation by the largest total overspend over any interval of consecutive rounds, which we call budget violation. Our algorithm, LEDGER, has $O(\sqrt T)$ expected regret and $O(\sqrt{T\log T})$ expected budget violation over $T$ rounds, uses one projection per round, and needs no strictly feasible action. The logarithm cannot be removed: with Gaussian noise of fixed positive variance, every algorithm with $O(\sqrt T)$ worst-case regret has worst-case budget violation of order at least $\sqrt{T\log T}$, even if only the final total overspend is counted, and budget violation $O(\sqrt T)$ forces linear regret. When violation is instead the sum of the positive parts of the per-round constraint values (hard violation), no algorithm keeps both expected regret and expected hard violation sublinear if the noise distribution is not fixed, even for affine constraints. With a fixed and known Gaussian noise law of standard deviation $σ$, a worst-case lower bound of order $\min\{σ,1\}T(\log\log T/\log T)^2$ shows that regret and hard violation cannot both be made polynomially sublinear. Noisy constraint values therefore still allow a signed budget to be controlled, at the cost of a logarithmic factor, but not the hard violation.

papers.title: From Synthetic Priors to Model Behavior: Structural Coverage in Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are commonly pretrained on large collections of procedurally generated synthetic tasks, yet it remains unclear how well these synthetic pretraining priors support the downstream tasks on which the models are evaluated. We study this from a distribution-level attribution perspective. We recover or reconstruct the synthetic data generators of four TFMs and compare their generated tasks with datasets from two widely used tabular benchmarks. Each dataset is represented by a common set of structural descriptors capturing schema, feature distributions, dependence structure, response properties, and feature--response relationships. We then measure how broadly and repeatedly each synthetic prior reaches benchmark tasks using structural coverage and normalized density, and examine whether stronger local support is associated with better predictive performance. We find substantial differences across synthetic pretraining priors: some generators provide broader and denser support for benchmark tasks than others. Moreover, stronger synthetic-to-benchmark support is generally associated with better relative model performance, although this association is largely driven by the model with the broadest support and mostly disappears once each model's average support is removed. These results suggest that structural coverage provides a useful diagnostic for characterizing synthetic pretraining priors, whereas its relationship to downstream model behavior mainly reflects differences between models and remains confounded with architecture and training.

papers.title: Robust and Sparse Group Dynamic Causal Modeling via Student-t Parametric Empirical Bayes and Nonlocal Priors
papers.abstract: Dynamic causal modeling (DCM) estimates directed effective connectivity, while parametric empirical Bayes (PEB) supports group inference using subject-specific posterior summaries. Standard PEB relies on Gaussian models and continuous shrinkage, making it sensitive to atypical estimates and unable to distinguish negligible from nonzero effects. We develop a robust and sparse group-DCM extension combining a Student-$t$ likelihood with a spike-and-slab prior using a nonlocal product-moment (pMOM) slab. A normal--gamma representation of the Student-$t$ distribution yields weights that downweight atypical {whitened residual coordinates}.
